name: Proportional representation
scope: Proportional representation as the political principle and reform programme that an elected assembly should reflect the distribution of votes, so that minorities are represented in proportion to their support, as Britannica defines it (s1), carried by the Electoral Reform Society's 1884 campaign (s2), FairVote's 'fair representation' (s3) and the political-representation literature (s4). Thinkers: Hare and Courtney (s1, s2), with Andrae and Mill named as originators of its methods (s1); text: Amy's Real Choices/New Voices (s3, s4). Covers the case for proportional outcomes, whatever the method (single transferable vote, party list, mixed-member). Excludes the detailed mechanics of any one counting formula, and single-winner reforms such as ranked-choice (alternative) voting for one seat.

summary: Proportional representation holds that an elected assembly should mirror how people voted, so that parties and minorities win seats in proportion to their support rather than the largest group taking the whole constituency. Its advocates argue that only an assembly reflecting the full diversity of opinion has legitimate decisions; critics reply that it encourages splinter parties and unstable government. It can be delivered by single transferable vote, party-list or mixed-member systems.
